A Time of War : A Memoir Across Three Generations

The air hangs heavy with the scent of gunpowder and fear. Across the continent, old alliances fracture as the Unified Monarchists and the Separatists clash for supremacy. Even in our quiet corner of the world, the drumbeat of war grows louder with every passing day.

Our father's work does not pause for the petty squabbles of kings and rebels, yet we cannot ignore the storm gathering at our doorstep. Whether we profit from the conflict or shield our estates from its fury, the choices we make in the coming years will echo across generations.

Word has reached the village that armies are marching through the neighboring provinces. In the taverns and the Town Hall, whispers of espionage, conscription, and fortune-making dominate every conversation.

Representatives from both factions have been spotted in the region, each seeking coin, supplies, and loyalty. Soon, our village will be forced to declare where it stands.

Plagued by Conflict

If one can call the prospect of perpetual conflict stabilizing, my life settled into a somewhat steady routine. During the day, the sound of distant gunfire rumbled through the halls of my estate as silver plumes of smoke billowed beyond the mountainous horizon, casting tendril-like shadows across the land — a constant reminder of civil war. At night, the rare spectacle of an explosion brightening the sky surprised me with how viscerally I reacted.

Soldiers in their bright regalia keep watch over the town from a newly erected outpost, waving the brilliant orange flag of royalty. The Monarchy had claimed victory from afar after stationing their ranks across the region, but as scuffles remained constant, this declaration was all pomp without substance. The Monarchy drafted citizens into their ranks and levied penalties against those who showed disloyalty.

The inference that one of my standing should owe a debt of servitude to those who already tax my earnings into oblivion was enough to make me spill my tea. And to what end, I wondered? Could peace be mustered in a populace kept so distant from the individuals who ruled it? It was called the industrial revolution for a reason, was it not?

But, I must admit, the safety that the Monarchy afforded appealed to my pocketbook. Appeasing the Monarchy would ensure money and influence, but it also appeared — for better or ill — that royalty was distant enough to take little interest in our experimentations unless they provided direct benefit to themselves, whereas the Separatists were interested in knowledge and were desperate to explore all scientific options available to them to turn the tide. However, their frail sensibilities would not so easily accept my experimentations.

Ah, to be left to one's own devices or to be famously scrutinized, reviled, and revered in equal measure! The decision weighed upon me so heavily it gave me mild indigestion during my evening banquets. What direction should I choose to advance my most important scientific work?
Down with the Monarchy

The length and difficulty of my journey was exacerbated by the ongoing conflict. Compounding this harried inconvenience, my spouse and I suffered the indignity of a lengthy interrogation by soldiers of the Separatist forces, who had imposed an unofficial martial government.

Peasants-turned-soldiers in their motley uniforms keep watch over the town from a newly erected outpost waving a sanguine flag. They spoke of freedom as they dug fresh graves in the cemetery, the wrought iron gates perpetually wreathed in lilies. I observed the daily horse-drawn carts, dragging the wounded towards ill-equipped infirmaries, my crimson reflection in the muddy ruts of unpaved highways.

It was both in spite of and because of this brashness that I found myself drawn to the scrappy Separatist upstarts and their eagerness to fight for the capricious whims of the great unwashed. Behind the Curve

My close friends and family - many of whom I have permanently severed contact with because of their feelings on the matter - have expressed extreme misgivings about the publication of this book. They claim that my macabre fascination with exposing this to the world is unhealthy!

Some have even derisively labeled this work as pseudoscience, homeopathy, or a drug-induced fever dream, but I say to them, "who are you to criticize the moon and the stars for being in the sky?" This work is important! How can they not see it? If anything, these outlandish experiments further prove the relevance of the science that is far better researched, performed, and peer-reviewed after publication in respected journals.

For while the world may have sped onward at a pace that our scientific contributions could not match, rendering our innovations lame and timid in comparison, I believe that my family's failure to make an impact on a world of the future is an important lesson. Our contributions must be remembered, not for their value to the progress of mankind, but for laying the foundations of the work that others would ignore because of other more viable innovations which they could hone to perfection.

The world may have progressed beyond a need for mad science, but I believe it is this spirit that will define my family's legacy. Even if what they did, does not.

A Brighter Future

While the discovery of my family's experiments and journals would cement my scientific ambitions for years to come, I had never actually met them. I was too young to remember the disappearance of my brilliant progenitor. To lose a parent and then another to the subsequent dementia that followed was more folly than one child should ever have to bear. I was shielded from this reality, rushed away to Vienna, where I was consumed by my studies until my twenty-first year. It was only at my partner's insistence that I decided to settle my inheritance.

I remember being stunned as I arrived by train on a mid-summer's evening. I do not know what I expected from the anecdotes my nanny had relayed to me, but it was not the bustling cityscape that greeted me. As the sun dipped into the forest, the glimmer of modern steel light fixtures amplified the urban luminescence. My delighted spouse and I enjoyed a quiet ride in our steamer car, which offered us a chance to observe the idyllic community and decidedly pleasant folk enjoying the convenience of electricity and steam turbine technology.

The estate appeared untouched by years of vacancy - recently pruned brambles and ivy adorned the iron gate and the expansive grounds were immaculate. A caretaker of great age and a small housekeeping staff greeted us. Although updating the grounds to the more modern standard of the nearby town would prove a daunting task, the servants' warm reception allayed our remaining anxieties. Upon discovery of my family's laboratory, what had been planned as a mere visit received an indefinite extension.

When I spoke of my family's history of experimentation, I was rarely met with indifference but more often firm words of encouragement. It appeared that this region, so rife with abnormal progress, viewed my theories as rudimentary but delightfully avant-garde. Even when I expounded upon dark rituals and the grotesque, they encouraged further exploration and referred me to the newly constructed University.

This caused me severe consternation. Was this not what I wanted — a clear path towards scientific enlightenment and support of my family's landmark ideas? Why did their lack of friction vex me so? Did they view my illustrious work as trivial?

It was this grim realization that strengthened my will. If these craven modernists wanted more, then so be it! I would push the limits of science further than ever before and damn the consequences!
Unexplainable Phenomenon
There is no taming the wiles of time. History abhors a paradox. Though I did not fully understand the significance, fascinating oddities began to appear when loopholes were left untied.
Advanced Work is Important!

While the journal was an astonishing discovery in itself, I did not realize that the true revelation would arrive several weeks later while I sampled brandy upon my veranda. A swirl of stormclouds suddenly converged overhead, and with a spear of electricity a fantastic metal contraption appeared. The {{0=|two|three|four|five}} travelers emerged, wrinkles lining their features and gray, wispy hair held back by jeweler's goggles strapped to their heads.

Our meeting was brief, but over a brunch of polenta and egg-plant stuffed with forcemeat, they relinquished control of several new schematics which they claimed had been retrieved from the future and would revolutionize the modern world. As one may have surmised from this encounter, the intrepid traveler was none other than my long-lost parent, here to entrust one final piece of my legacy.

With these experiments, they implored, I could work towards a true Utopia - a world of technological perfection.
The Future of Convenience

These schematics weren't exactly what I had envisioned as a chilling and ethically dubious leap into the future of science, but they were certainly handy around the house.

If one could procure the additional materials required to create them, I was convinced that these devious advanced devices would allow me to achieve the proper recognition I deserved.
Nostalgic Guests

I wasn't quite sure why the mantle in my study was adorned with a small metal {{0=Sickle or Shield}}. As with much of the decor, I allowed my spouse free reign over matters of interior decoration, and thought nothing of it until a dinner guest became enamored with its presence.

He doffed his top hat and brass monocle to put the object to closer inspection. "I thought they had all been destroyed after the war so many years ago. Curious that you would proudly display such a vulgar symbol of aggression!"

Little did I realize the rumors I would soon endure from this singular supper event.

New Science

When I discovered the journal, the masterwork plans, and the clandestine fragments of experiments in the laboratory, I laughed. Surely, my great-grandfather had grandiose ambitions at the time, but modern advancements made many of the blueprints obsolete and frankly, a bit cute.

I decided to improve upon them, and I knew just the thing that would dazzle them all!
Rediscovered Artist

An art critic arrived at my estate, and immediately took an enthusiastic interest in the misshapen wooden figure.

He explained his theory on the authenticity of the artistic piece: "His more well-known work in marble defined most of his career, however we believe that Ferenczy explored an abstract modernist period well before his contemporaries, with wooden figures."

The collector offered me $2 for the misshapen wooden figure, a sum that I gladly accepted in order to be rid of the hideous thing.
The Key

I noticed that the misshapen wooden figure felt hollow inside. With a moment's hesitation, I cracked the object against the corner of the table. The contents spilled out upon the floor.

The object inside could not exist, and yet there it was. My mind was filled with questions that I knew might never be fully answered, but I was thankful for the assistance.
Time Machine - Publication?

While the ideas set forth in my parent's journal entries were both outdated and embarrassingly rudimentary in some areas, one thing that the fools in academia hounded us to provide was the schematics to the Time Conveyance Device. For a discovery so radical and immense in its influence on multiple dimensions of the world, the meager sums they offered for entrusting it to their universities was insulting.

I would never give it to them to abuse secretly at their discretion. No! But to publish it widely and allow all of the Hungarian people the chance to rewrite history? That, it seemed, would be the sort of experimental chaos the stuffed shirts at the university would never see coming!

But, perhaps, and most undoubtably, it would have untold repercussions.

The issue at hand, however, was the matter of secrecy. If any one of us - myself or my dear cousins - decided to publish the schematic, it would be freely available.

I knew that each would need to make their own private decision and I prayed that it would be the correct choice.

A white-haired woman emerged from the chemical mist, clutching her side. The elderly lady was dressed in metallic attire that was both intriguing and exotic. The shiny material was frayed as though some impossibly large claws had shredded it, while splatters of liquid (much of it dark red) adorned her outfit. While the journal of my parents was an astonishing discovery in itself, I did not realize that the true revelation would arrive several weeks later when I rifled through the pages willed to me. I suspect that you may assume that my memory had slipped or that I had not been thorough in my studies of those browning pages locked within the cellar laboratory, but I swear by my blood to be true.

I had read over the myriad notes and journal entries so many times that I had memorized their contents, yet one afternoon when I turned to a central page, several pristine and folded pieces of parchment fell to the floor. A faint and acrid scent of burnt oil wafted from the papers, which each detailed a new, amazing schematic for devices far more advanced than any I had ever perceived possible.
The Future is NOW
